simple.meaning: פָּצַר (pâtsar) is a Hebrew concept word meaning “to peck at , i.e. (figuratively) stun or dull.” BibleIQ follows how Scripture develops this idea across its occurrences.
simple.biblicalBackground: The concept appears 7 times across Genesis, Judges, 1 Samuel, 2 Kings, beginning at Genesis 19:3. Its contexts include birth, family, Torah, kingship.
simple.inThisVerse: In this verse, the tapped English word is source-aligned to פָּצַר (H6484).
simple.whyItMatters: Concept words shape biblical themes. BibleIQ keeps the concept grounded in actual verse evidence instead of starting with a later theological definition.

occurrences.englishText: He urged them greatly, and they came in with him, and entered into his house. He made them a feast, and baked unleavened bread, and they ate.

They said, “Stand back!” Then they said, “This one fellow came in to live as a foreigner, and he appoints himself a judge. Now we will deal worse with you than with them!” They pressed hard on the man Lot, and came near to break the door.
Please take the gift that I brought to you, because God has dealt graciously with me, and because I have enough.” He urged him, and he took it.
The man rose up to depart; but his father-in-law urged him, and he stayed there again.

For rebellion is as the sin of witchcraft, and stubbornness is as idolatry and teraphim.* teraphim were household idols that may have been associated with inheritance rights to the household property. Because you have rejected Yahweh’s word, he has also rejected you from being king.”
When they urged him until he was ashamed, he said, “Send them.”
But he said, “As Yahweh lives, before whom I stand, I will receive none.”
